title: Tulane University (Tulane Lakeside Hospital for Women and Children)
paragraphs: Introduction. University of California Davis (2017/03/20 - 2017/03/30), Tulane University (2017/04/03 - 2017/04/28), University of Western Australia (2017/05/01 - 2017/06/23). These are the very valuable opportunities I was given thanks to the International Collaboration Office, the Academic Affairs Division, the Frontier Society, and the doctors and seniors who built this study abroad system into what it is. I sincerely thank them. Thank you very much.

From preparation to departure. It was an opportunity that I had wished for myself and finally obtained after much preparation, but "my first long stay overseas, and moreover going into a medical setting to do something" was enough to fill me with anxiety at first. Starting from studying for the TOEFL, I learned medical vocabulary in English and practiced outputting it. No matter how much I did, I could not be sure how much would be required of me locally and how much I could use. Besides that, I had many worries, such as how the mobile phone signal, means of transportation and public safety would be, but I also feel that, for that reason, I was able to prepare thoroughly. Thinking a lot and preparing a lot. This work was itself both an anxiety and a good time of nonstop excitement.

Clerkship at Tulane Lakeside Hospital for women and children. I had put in pediatrics and gastroenterology as my preferred departments, so I never imagined that they would accept me in ped GI (pediatric gastroenterology). However, when I actually went, more than half of my schedule was empty slots. Having made various preparations, gone through procedures and come all the way from Japan, I could not spend more than half of it idle; I had to do something. My first task was to get the schedule changed. Somehow I pleaded my case, and a one-week schedule was completed with general ped (general pediatrics), the well-baby nursery, a place that manages babies born without particular problems, small participatory classes called preceptors, and so on. Thanks to that, I was blessed with good doctors and was given the role of pediatric checkups, history taking, physical examination, and then conveying it. I was very grateful to be given the chance to take histories and perform physical examinations, in front of the parents, as a student for whom English is a second language. For that reason, I cannot forget the tension when knocking on the door and entering the room. In the preceptor, the local students put forward opinions and spoke up one after another, which overwhelmed me. I spoke up too in an effort to leave some mark, but I felt frustrated with conditions that I could explain in Japanese but could not express well in English. On the other hand, they were very impressed that I was studying medicine in a second language, and I thought, so there is such a way of looking at it, which was fresh.

Although it is not a partner school... I was also allowed to go to University of California Davis Dermatology for only ten days. Dermatology in the United States is extremely competitive and very difficult to get into. Although as an observer, I am very glad to have been able to experience that atmosphere. What surprised me was that there are many patients with psoriasis and actinic keratosis. I was also surprised by the difference in patients' attitude toward preventing actinic keratosis and squamous cell carcinoma. Not a medical matter, but the doctor who looked after me most was affable, calm and treated me very sincerely. He was greatly admired by the residents and students, and this person's atmosphere, way of speaking and way of dealing with people were things to learn from, and I think they influenced my image of a future doctor not a little.

Fiona Stanley Hospital acute surgery unit (ASU). The week after finishing the Tulane University clerkship, the clerkship at Fiona Stanley Hospital ASU began. The ASU is where people who need surgery in the acute phase, or may need it, are, and there were many people with cholecystitis, appendicitis, small bowel obstruction, acute pancreatitis and diverticulitis. The students' main roles were ward rounds and assisting in operations. Occasionally I received lectures, took histories and did physical examinations, but students were more or less free to move as they liked. Besides operations, I also attended classes with the local students. It is basically 'It's up to you.', so unless I approach actively on my own what I can do now, what I can learn and what actions I should take, nothing begins. Of course, it was not always that things went well when I approached actively, but as an exchange student from overseas, I decided, in a good sense, to throw away embarrassment and take on challenges boldly. I feel that this experience has greatly influenced how I conduct myself in Japan now.

Sir Charles Gairdner Hospital Vascular Surgery. The clerkship here was spent all day with the registrars and fellows. Every day started with rounds, followed by operations, catheter procedures and responding to people who came in as emergencies. (On days with outpatient clinic, we split into two groups and did them at the same time.) The operations were amputation (toe, below knee, above knee), endarterectomy, bypass and abscess drainage, and the catheter procedures were angioplasty, atherectomy, EVAR, TEVAR, angiogram and so on. Registrars and fellows are in positions of working very busily in Australia, and thanks to following those doctors all the time, there were cases in which I could see everything from admission to discharge. It was a case in which a patient arrived by ambulance, an emergency bypass was performed, the next day steal syndrome arose from the bypass vessel so the causative vessel was occluded by catheter, the next day compartment syndrome arose so fasciotomy was done, and a few days later the circulation of the lower limb improved. I think I could see all these procedures precisely because I was with them all the time. In catheter procedures, I also received detailed explanations next to the radiology technologist. Personally, the biggest event was giving a presentation on moyamoya disease at a conference attended even by consultants. They watched over me warmly, but the tension of presenting in a foreign land was great.

What is the significance of studying abroad? I thought about it before departure and throughout, but I cannot think of a single phrase that feels right. To learn the differences in medicine between overseas and Japan? Language ability? Broadening my perspective? If any one of them were the main reason alone, it would seem insufficient. This opportunity, built with time, money and effort and on enormous support, is meaningful, isn't it, in exploring as much as one can obtain? And then digesting, absorbing and using what was obtained through that exploration for one's future conduct. I think that is what matters. It was not all enjoyable, but if I were asked whether I would want to go again, I would answer 100% that I would go again. Finally, I will keep working hard without forgetting that I was given such an opportunity and that I am an extremely fortunate person. Thank you.
